#9864. A simple logo redesign has become Australia's latest culture war – why that's bad news for designers

A simple logo redesign has become Australia's latest culture war – why that's bad news for designers

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you'd asked me last month to name the most politically explosive branding project in Australia, I wouldn't have guessed it'd be a local council's email signature.
  • Sutherland Shire Council, in Sydney's south, covers a population of around 240,000 people.
  • Yet in recent weeks, it's been at the centre of a row over its crest: an engraved portrait of Captain James Cook, who first came ashore on Australia's east coast at Kurnell, within the shire, in 1770.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you'd asked me last month to name the most politically explosive branding project in Australia, I wouldn't have guessed it'd be a local council's email signature. But here we are.

Sutherland Shire Council, in Sydney's south, covers a population of around 240,000 people. It rarely gets much coverage in the national press, let alone grabs attention in England over 10,000 miles away.

Yet in recent weeks, it's been at the centre of a row over its crest: an engraved portrait of Captain James Cook, who first came ashore on Australia's east coast at Kurnell, within the shire, in 1770.

Back in July, staff began favouring a newer, simpler logo across its communications. It's a light blue wave that's simple but effectively represents an area on Australia's east coast.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, Cook has not been "cancelled", removed or erased by the council. They've simply moved the emblem featuring him to what they call "civic, ceremonial and high-value corporate applications", while using the newer one for things like email signatures, where a simpler mark works better.

Councillor Haris Strangas, though, wasn't happy that he'd never been asked about this change. So he tabled a motion to review the council's policy, then went on the Today show, a major national breakfast TV programme in Australia, to discuss what he'd done.

Industry observers note that admittedly, in the clip, Haris came across as a likeable, ordinary guy who said he didn't want to inflame the issue and acknowledged most people have better things to talk about. Nonetheless, he wasn't backing down, and as a result, Sutherland Shire found itself a front in Australia's long-running culture wars. Lots of other people then piled in with their own agendas, and you can imagine how it's all spiralled out of control since.

While I imagine most people in the area simply shook their heads and ignored this episode, I think it says something about how politics is making it harder for designers to do their jobs.

According to recent reports, logos are tools, not monuments. They need to be tweaked, updated, redesigned or replaced when they start to look tired, or for practical reasons, like when they don't work on small screens. It's not vandalism; it's maintenance.

Industry observers note that ninety-nine per cent of the time, this happens, and nobody bats an eyelid when logo redesigns get it right. Mastercard dropped its name from its circles emblem in 2019. Volkswagen flattened its badge the same year. Burger King reverted to its retro bun in 2021. Pepsi brought back a bolder, blacker globe in 2023. Few people outside the Creative Bloq audience would ever have noticed.

Even changes to the Sunderland Shire logo followed the same pattern. In 2008 the council shrank Cook in favour of its name and a latest colour scheme. Ahead of the 250th anniversary of Cook's landing, it restyled the portrait for digital screens. The wave itself was introduced back in 2017. None of this made the national news.

So what's changed? Well, sadly, we're in an era when a rebrand isn't just a rebrand. If people can make it a symbol of something bigger, they will. It's no longer about colours, type or kerning. It's about identity.

None of this means history doesn't matter, or that communities shouldn't have a say in how they're represented. But let's be clear: Cook has not been, and has not been, erased. The council just introduced a different design for specific use cases. That's all.

The fuss that people make over such minor tweaks puts designers in a difficult position. The lesson many clients will take from this, Cracker Barrel, Jaguar et al is that it's safer never to change anything at all. That's bad for design, and frankly bad for the organisations themselves, which end up stuck with identities that no longer work.

Sources indicate that tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FALLEN STAR. Sotheby’s is pushing back against an 11th-hour restitution claim for its star lot, an estimated $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting, reports ARTnews. The heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher whose family fled Nazi Germany, asked Sotheby’s to withdraw the painting from its Wednesday auction and prove that it was not sold under duress. However, what constitutes duress is up for debate. One indicator is whether a painting sold for a fair price, which, according to latest details, appears to have been the case. The auction house told ARTnews that the Fischer family sold the Van Gogh in question, Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), for 68,000 Swiss francs, or about $22,000, through a dealer in June 1936. The sale took place in the Netherlands, when it was not yet occupied by the Nazis. That price was a relatively strong one at the time. However, the family’s lawyers point out that the heirs were already on the run from by then from the Nazis, who had begun banning the family’s publishing house from printing many of its authors. The sale, they claim, would not have happened under normal circumstances. SCHOOL’S OUT. The fresh Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has its critics, ARTnews’s own Maximilíano Durón being one of them. But lately, new concerns have been raising eyebrows. For one, the institution is keeping its outdoor plaza around the museum permanently closed off, despite it being intended as “a generous civic space,” as ARTnews reported. More recently, we’ve learned from L.A. Material, that a promised education program, touted as central to the museum’s mission and a key reason it was granted a 99-year lease on public land at the rate of $30 annually, is nowhere in sight. One explanation is that about a year ago, the museum fired most of its education department. Now, its newly built classrooms are kept closed to the public, there is no sign the museum is looking to hire replacements, and local educators have been left ghosted. A follow-up story in the Los Angeles Times quotes a museum spokesperson stating: “We’re actively plotting our overall programming slate, and kids- and family-focused offerings will be included in that rollout in 2027.” At this stage, the museum is already far short of what it told local authorities, including that the museum would launch its education program prior to opening, for children of all ages. In a statement to LA Material, the museum spokesperson added that the future educational program would now “be focused on older students.”.

It has been revealed that margot Heller, the director of the South London Gallery, is stepping down after 25 years on the job. [ARTnews].

A stolen sculpture of a metal bird by the artist Helen Denerley, intended to be sold for charity, was returned to where it was exhibited in Inverness, Scotland, along with an apology and a £100 ($132) donation. [BBC].

In a recent development, during a Saturday ceremony, the artist Lotus L. Kang was named the winner of the 2026 Sobey Art Award, which comes with $70,000. [The Art Newspaper].

According to recent reports, germany’s federal government has budgeted over €2.58 billion ($2.84 billion) towards culture and media in 2027, but behind the numbers observers warn that relatively little funding is going toward contemporary art. [Monopol Magazine].

In a recent development, HAD ME AT HOT CHOCOLATE BAR. The latest, £437 million ($576.8 million) London Museum is opening November 28, and its director spills on all it will have to offer in an interview with the Times of London. Admittedly, we are particularly intrigued by plans for a 24-hour hot chocolate bar. The so-called “temperance Cocoa Room,” open all night, and museum hours until 11 p.m. and midnight, are some plans that Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, hopes to implement at the institution’s new home, a renovated 800-year-old meat market. Temperance rooms were created in the 19th century to provide non-alcoholic beverage options, and one such room focused on hot chocolate was discovered at the museum site during construction and subsequently preserved. “We are reviving that idea of a meeting place for people who would prefer a hot chocolate to a beer,” mentioned Ament. “And I want it to be open all night, even if there’s only me in there.”.

Industry News: 'It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person': Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band.
  • It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art.
  • Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative.

Industry observers note that “It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she notes. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali claims. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”.

Industry observers note that informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she states.“This is notable in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”.

Recent findings suggest that as for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”.

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

Recent findings suggest that I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?

My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

In a recent development, november is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago.
  • Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • It has been revealed that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not latest, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

It has been revealed that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

For some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

Industry observers note that “It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” states Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

Patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting upcoming collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is swiftly becoming the preferred method.

Sources indicate that “[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” indicates Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

This type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” indicates Dr. Pearl.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

While there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

In a recent development, try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

It has been revealed that for cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

Industry observers note that but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” claims Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

According to recent reports, if injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers, a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world.
  • Rare are the times when a New York museum has turned over an entire floor to a presentation of digital art.
  • Industry observers note that the titular artport is an online gallery launched in 2001 by curator Christiane Paul, who has since gone on to commission plenty of works in the intervening 25 years, by artists ranging from JODI to Mimi Ọnụọha.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: This story is part of Newsmakers, a new ARTnews series where we interview the movers and shakers who are making change in the art world.

Rare are the times when a New York museum has turned over an entire floor to a presentation of digital art. That makes “artport: A History of Internet Art,” opening at the Whitney Museum on Saturday, an outlier in the institution’s programming—and something of a major occasion.

Industry observers note that the titular artport is an online gallery launched in 2001 by curator Christiane Paul, who has since gone on to commission plenty of works in the intervening 25 years, by artists ranging from JODI to Mimi Ọnụọha. Officially indexed as part of the Whitney collection since 2015, artport continues to commission artists. The most recent was Jazsalyn, who, for one work staged earlier this year, proposed what she called “Black Metatheories” as means of forming something alternative to AI and called on people to respond to a range of prompts, including one that reads: “Consider blackness. How does life persist within the spectrum of impossible possibility?” Related Articles Frieze's Kristell Chadé Discusses Why the Fair Has 'Never Been About Adding Points on a Map' Newsmakers: Studio Ma's Christiana Moss on Building Museums for a Hotter, More Expensive World.

Artport’s offerings live on the Whitney’s website. Generally, however, they have not been show in the Whitney’s galleries, something that will change with Paul’s exhibition opening this week, which features more than works associated with artport. The show is yet another digital art–focused exhibition from one of the great thinkers on the subject. She literally wrote the book on digital art in 2003, and is currently in the process of writing a follow-up to it.

ARTnews spoke with Paul, a curator of digital art at the Whitney, to learn more about artport’s history and how she created such an ambitious show. This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Sources indicate that ARTnews: Artport was founded in 2001, but it didn’t become a part of the Whitney’s collection until 2015. More than 10 years later, what is its place at the Whitney today?

According to recent reports, christiane Paul: I would not say it’s changed much. The original thinking, which we kept intact, was: It’s kind of weird to lock down net art in a collection. And that is why we decided to commission the works under non-exclusive licenses. But what changed in 2015 was really that we wanted to acknowledge the artist’s status in all of this. By making it officially its own little umbrella collection within the permanent collection, all of the artists gained lifetime membership status, and are now treated the same way as collection artists—that wasn’t the case before.

Also, the works are of course more integrated into the collection database. Before, when you searched, everything was there on artport, but it did not necessarily appear in collection searches, which also became problematic when we added more physical works by some of the artists—for example, a sculpture by Auriea Harvey [whose work was commissioned by artport in 2023]—to the collection. You would find the sculpture, but not the rest of her work.

When artport commissions an artist—let’s say, for its “On the Hour” series, which stages projects on the Whitney’s website at designated times—who is the commissioner, the Whitney or artport?

The commissioner is always the Whitney Museum, and I invite artists to submit a proposal. What we don’t do is show existing work. We did a series from 2009 to 2023, “Sunrise Sunset,” that marked sunrise and sunset through a 30-second intervention into whitney.org that played on all pages. I found the format highly intriguing, because it’s so net art to disrupt, particularly an institutional website. While it was very beautiful and poetic, there also was a concern: This was sunrise and sunset, Newly introduced York time only. That prompted us to change it to make it into hourly interventions.

My invitations to “On the Hour” are often based on two criteria. First of all, who are artists who can really work with that kind of seriality intervention, in terms of vignettes? I think it’s also a great way to give younger artists a chance to do something for the museum. In general, artport has always paid a lot of attention to emerging artists, but due to the format, this lends itself to being a little more experimental.

In a recent development, what did you look for when you started commissioning artists? How did you know an artist was good for artport?

Sources indicate that the main goal of artport was always to show the breadth of practice in the in the online field. When artport was launched in 2001, of course, there already was a history of net art. I mean, depending on if you’re counting by accessibility to the public, the internet launched in 1993. Artistic practice in this space started around that time and really took off in the mid-’90s. So, by the time I started, there was already a backlog of the artists who were creating the language of the field: Mark Napier, Tina La Porta, Martin Wattenberg, Marek Walczak, Amy Alexander. I was rapidly moving through those people at the time. Then I was following who was doing significant work in that area.

Industry observers note that certainly, when you started artport, institutions had already begun paying attention to net art. Documenta X in 1997 had a net art section, and Lawrence Rinder organized a net art portion of the 2000 Whitney Biennial. You did something similar for the 2002 edition, and Rhizome partnered with the Newly introduced Museum in 2003. But it seems like we’re in a very different moment now, where net art can even be the subject of major exhibitions like the artport one. What does it mean, now, to bring net art into museum walls?

I would once again say my approach has not changed that much. There’s more technological support for doing these types of demonstrates, so the infrastructural possibilities and budget certainly did change. But since the ’90s, there has been this discussion of: “Oh, this should only be seen online.” I always thought that was such an ironic misunderstanding because online is not on your couch in your house. Online is everywhere! We’re online in the museum. People are on their phones. Everything is networked.

It has been revealed that you’re definitely changing the context [by showing it in a museum], but it’s important to see this art in the context of other art forms, and that was very important to me. The challenge that an exhibition like this poses is: How do you make the work easily accessible within a gallery space while also maintaining its net-ness? On the one hand, it’s about not overwhelming people with dozens and dozens of screens, which we do still have in this exhibition. But we’re also changing formats quite a bit, and at the same time, we’re not sucking out what the online environment is really about.

How did you maintain that net-ness?

Sources indicate that the way I approached it with this exhibition was to use an open floor and a landscape of browser windows as a design conceit. There are floating walls held up by poles. There’s also a lot of cabling, as you can imagine. The walls or panels suggest open browser windows on which the screens are presented. They’re not segregating works into rooms—they’re all the web, where you might switch from one tab to another. Some works have been translated into more of an installation, like Andy Deck’s Screening Circle [2006], for example, which you use online, with different people contributing to it. You use your mouse to choose pixels and create an icon within this screening circle. And in the gallery, you will see it projected onto a platform with actually four tablets for input, so four people can use it simultaneously. It will switch between them and also bring in the online work.

According to recent reports, there are also works that have components of paintings or prints, like Michael Mandiberg, for example. They did an endurance performance, Life Study [2018], where, over the course of four years, they filmed themself doing paintings of their assistants. We’re not only showing the work and its archive, but also some of the paintings.

The exhibition is titled “artport: A History of Internet Art,” which suggests that it is a history of net art, and that there are others still to be told. What is the history you’re telling?

Julia Kaganskiy puts it nicely in her essay for the catalog. There are timestamps that are demarcating the concerns, attitudes, social norms, and media environments that have shaped our collective lives. I think any type of net art that one would have picked beyond artport from the ’90s until today would somehow tell that history. Of course, the history that artport tells is a very specific one in that there are certain choices of artists, and they tell that history in a specific way, through their personal lens. If it were a completely different roster of artists, those timestamps marking these shifts would still be there, but the story would be told slightly differently.

There’s also a fresh performance by the artist duo Operator: the third act of their ongoing “Human Unreadable” project, begun in 2022.

Operator has, for the past four years, created the series “Human Unreadable,” which is a generative choreography on the blockchain. It’s open source, so that people can use to do their own performances. In Act I, they translated sequences that were created by the choreography into large-scale black and white images that were sold as NFTs. In Act II, collectors could reveal the movement sequence that had generated the image. From the start, the work raised the question: How much of the body survives translation into code? In Act III, we have bodies without the mediation of the screen performing the first 100 tokens choreographic sequences. It really is a multimedia theater piece that also includes spoken word, and it is really about our relationships to technological systems, the artist’s personal story, and negotiating ambition and technology in your life. And its two matinees are live streamed: I think we now have 18 partner institutions. The live stream is not simply “Oh, here is a camera that shows you what’s happening at the Whitney.” It is more of an artwork in and of itself, with moving cameras and modifications, almost a little bit more like Nam June Paik’s Good Morning, Mr. Orwell minus the technological difficulties. [Laughs.].

It has been revealed that A lot of younger viewers who encounter this exhibition may not entirely understand everything involved in creating the early net art surveyed here—for example, the splash pages produced for artport between 2001 and 2006, which rely on a technology that is generally out of use in our current internet. How will you contextualize those pieces for viewers less familiar with them?

It has been revealed that there were 57 splash pages—they were done monthly—and I am only showing the ones where artists created standalone projects rather than just a splash page or gate page for their work, because that kind of browsing is better done at home. The intention is to get lost in an artist’s work and website, and that would really distract from the focus of the exhibition. That being said, we are explaining the functionality of splash pages and what they were in the section text. But I hope the art of that time, and the environment of the web at the time, really translates—to me, that is actually the most significant part of the exhibition. There are these really nice connections across the floor between these early works and later ones that show you how really our attitudes towards self-representation, identity, surveillance data processing have shifted over time.

Industry observers note that there’s an early work by Jillian McDonald that was made 20 years before deepfakes. It’s about fan culture—she inserted herself into the film Buffalo ’66 with Vincent Gallo. I have it right across from works by Tina La Porta, who did voyeur_web [2001] at a time when live casting was so popular. People would put up webcams in their homes, in their kitchens, in their bedrooms, as this kind of gesture of returning the gaze, something that people wouldn’t do anymore today. It’s a completely different attitude that gets reflected in Maya Man‘s A Realistic Day in My Life Living in Newly introduced York City [2024–25], which takes this highly stylized TikTok culture of a supposedly realistic day that is completely performed and provides a counterpoint to what voyeur_web did.

The freedom that some of this early net artists had is amazing. It’s just not possible anymore, with so much of the internet became commodified, capitalized, and cleaner.

It has been revealed that what really struck me in reviving some of the older pieces was that the first generation of net artists really used the web as material, in terms of scraping and reprocessing. The access they had, you don’t have that anymore with the corporate lockdown.

According to recent reports, and you had to have a certain degree of technical know-how, too. I was rereading a 2015 interview you did with the artist Marisa Olson for Rhizome in which you stated you were dubious that net art still existed. Do you still feel that way?

I would slightly revise my framing. [Laughs.] What I was really getting at was that in the ’90s or early 2000s, you really had a category of net artists. Those were people who really worked with the web, and that was it—that was their practice. And I think with so-called post-internet, post-digital art, this crossed over into more material form, even though the internet was still at the core of the practice. In the sense of the net artist who does work online, and that is the practice, period? I think that is much harder to find today. You still have net art, and a lot of it. I mean, Maya Man, Chia Amisola are younger artists who are really doing net art in the spirit of the online environment, but Maya also does very material works. Artists have been branching out more: They may be doing work on the web and in sculpture painting across the board. You might argue that has changed in contemporary art in general, which has become less medium-specific. But there is still net art.

How AdHoc made Dispatch feel like an animated TV series

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that dispatch looks, sounds, and plays like an animated TV show, and that was deliberate: AdHoc wanted it to be a no-barrier entry point for people who don't usually play games.
  • Recent findings suggest that the game stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as Robert Robertson, a former hero turned dispatcher for a team of reformed supervillains, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast.
  • You can read how four video tracks and a doughnut shop gave Dispatch its start, but here I ask co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO, and both co-creative directors, how they nailed down the premium animation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dispatch looks, sounds, and plays like an animated TV show, and that was deliberate: AdHoc wanted it to be a no-barrier entry point for people who don't usually play games. A year after its launch on 22 October 2025, the episodic superhero workplace comedy has more than five million players, and the new Dispatch Deluxe Edition offers new ways to play, including replacing its graphics with storyboard art.

Recent findings suggest that the game stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as Robert Robertson, a former hero turned dispatcher for a team of reformed supervillains, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. Getting that cast to feel like they're in the same room, and getting the player to feel part of the story, took a lot of invisible work.

You can read how four video tracks and a doughnut shop gave Dispatch its start, but here I ask co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO, and both co-creative directors, how they nailed down the premium animation.

It has been revealed that how do you keep dialogue, facial expressions and performances consistent when the player can send a scene in different directions? While it was made using Unreal Engine 5, it starts on the page. "Everything is written with choice in mind," says Herman.

Sources indicate that adHoc built its own tools to ingest scripts, including a playable script you can read and click through. That produces the recording script actors use in the booth, which Herman claims is "a little bit crazy to read on a linear page". Do it long enough, though, and it starts to make sense. Each scene has a spine, and every time a choice appears, different options eventually trunk back into the main flow.

Recent findings suggest that the studio also uses recordings as a directing tool. AdHoc ingests every performance as it’s captured, so when an actor records opposite someone already in the booth, the team can play those existing lines back for them to react to. In Herman’s example, with Aaron Paul already recorded, the team can bring in Erin as Blonde Blazer, play Paul’s lines for her to read off, then play him again after her response. It’s a clever bit of craft: AdHoc builds each conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman claims, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they’re coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

It's clever craft. Rather than recording actors in isolation and hoping the performances fit together later, AdHoc builds the conversation around real delivery. The effect, Herman says, is to simulate the actors being in the same room, which helps performances feel grounded and integrated. It also gives a scene its flow, because the actors know where they're coming in from, and it makes testing branches easy.

It has been revealed that by the time animation begins, the voice work is trusted, and the team is happy with it. The facial animation then comes down to knowing every character. "Not everyone laughs the same. When they cry, they look different," Herman indicates. "Every character is their own person. Like they are on the page, they are in animation." Getting there takes "a lot of review, a lot of ref", and the team shoots plenty of reference footage for its animators.

For AdHoc, the problem was the seam: the point where a cutscene ends and gameplay begins. “The goal was always to make it feel integrated,” Lenart says. Part of the studio’s philosophy is that gameplay and story should feel like a seamless handoff rather than two different experiences. He and Herman had worked on plenty of games with clear story sections and clear gameplay sections, “and you could feel that break every single time”. That, he says, “always kind of drove us crazy”.

According to recent reports, when they dreamed of starting their own studio, one mandate was to choose mechanics that feel like an integrated part of a character's life, not scenes contrived for interactivity. If someone has to break into a room and pick a lock, it shouldn't be something the character would never do.

Industry observers note that for Dispatch, that meant the shift mechanic. Robert sends heroes out on calls because it's his job. "It's the thing he does every day," states Lenart. "So, when he sits down at his computer to do it, it feels natural.".

The team also made sure the Z-Team keep talking to the player throughout each shift, so the dialogue and relationships keep flowing, and the story never stops for gameplay. At times, a shift cuts out to a cinematic and back in again, and Lenart claims that only feels organic because "we spent a lot of time and effort to make it that way".

Herman and Lenart both spent years at Telltale Games, the studio behind The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands, and Dispatch forced them to drop much of their old way of working.

Industry observers note that at Telltale, Lenart says, cinematics were "fast and loose". Episodes were made in what the studio called live development: they would release one episode, then spend the next six weeks on the following. Things "could change at any time". Player feedback from the previous episode could feed straight back in, with tweaks to cinematics and character intentions right up until the day before shipping.

Sources indicate that dispatch had a different goal. AdHoc wanted the visuals and style to feel like "a premium animated television show" that wasn't a barrier for people who might enjoy a story like this but aren't typically into games. That meant a more traditional animation pipeline, with decisions made much earlier and, in some cases, locked down a year in advance.

"That was a really major learning curve for us since we were used to being able to make small adjustments all the way up until the last minute," Lenart says. But he now thinks the discipline made the game better. It "forced many detailed conversations way earlier in the process, which only better informed how each piece of the story was going to play out". His verdict: "Oh, this is actually the way to make the best quality product.".

The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners.

These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian debuted Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

#9858. After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York

After Exile, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s Prison Drawings Arrive in New York

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In one of Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s prison drawings, swans skim a swimming pool inside a cell.
  • Art that emerges from incarceration tends to speak first in material, with scarcity making resourcefulness something like a protagonist.
  • It has been revealed that ARTnews spoke with Otero Alcántara via email about his experience making art in prison, and settling into his second life in Miami.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In one of Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara’s prison drawings, swans skim a swimming pool inside a cell. In another, a clownish figure peers over the prison wall, perched with apparent ease on barbed wire. The Cuban artist and leader of the San Isidro Movement made thousands of such works in Guanajay, a maximum-security prison outside Havana, where he served time after his arrest on July 11, 2021, amid anti-government protests across the island. His release this year, after international outcry over creative freedom, was contingent on exile to the United States. A small selection of those works makes up “Tocar el cielo,” their first public showing, now at the Newly introduced York gallery Foreign & Domestic (curated by Alexander Meurice, and on view through December 13). Related Articles After Days of Uncertainty, Cuban Artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara Arrives in Miami Jailed Dissident Artist Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara Pens Appeal to 'People of Conscience' On Two-Year Anniversary of Arrest: 'Every Young Cuban Is a Political Prisoner'.

Art that emerges from incarceration tends to speak first in material, with scarcity making resourcefulness something like a protagonist. Otero Alcántara recounted drawing on drink cartons and cigarette packs, and smuggling in colored ink that ended up on other prisoners’ skin, when bodies were canvas enough. Who gets to make art inside, and who can get supplies to them, comes with its own politics. But he describes his five years in prison as one long performance, an “involuntary artistic gesture,” and the show reflects rather than transcribes the specifics of injustice. It’s an oblique testimony to how, bereft of sky or savior, the mind can slip its confines.

It has been revealed that ARTnews spoke with Otero Alcántara via email about his experience making art in prison, and settling into his second life in Miami. The following conversation has been translated from Spanish and condensed for publication.

ARTnews: How is your spirit these days? What has surprised you most about settling into life here?

In a recent development, luis Manuel Otero Alcántara: I think it’s been a shock. It’s unsettling, and it scares me a little.

According to recent reports, people outside Cuba could connect with my work, but it grew out of life in the neighborhood, out of my connection with the people there. Above all, it came from knowing that neighborhood called Cuba, that neighborhood called Havana, where I was like a fish in water.

Recent findings suggest that in Fresh York, I’m getting to know other ways of thinking, other ways of doing things. I’m learning how art relates to people here and how people relate to art. There’s the language barrier, too. In my own practice, I want art to disappear into the social fabric, into people’s lives. I want it to have a real effect on the person walking down the street.

Industry observers note that I feel like an embryo, like I’m learning from scratch how art and people relate to one another. So yes, it scares me. I’d call it a difficult process, but it’s a living process.

Sources indicate that can you tell me about making art in prison? How did you get supplies, and when did you work? What did materials typically cost you?

I started making art the moment I set foot in prison. They put me in a punishment cell, and I spent about two or three months there. Before prison, I was detained more than 50 times in three years. Even if they only held me for two or three days, I always made something in the cell. At first, I didn’t have the materials I had later. When I finished a drink my family had brought me, I’d keep the carton and draw on it. I used cigarette packs too. I’d stitch them together to make a surface I could draw on.

Industry observers note that once the materials from home ran out, my friends sent me more. When I called, all those friends of mine—Yanelys Núñez, Claudia Genlui, Coco Fusco, Camila Lobón, Anamely Ramos—picked up the phone. That was an act of resistance and an act of friendship. They took money they could have spent on food or on things they needed and used it to send me good art supplies, really good ones, all the way to Cuba, into the prison where I was being held.

That’s what I mean by cultural resistance. For my friends, it meant keeping the art alive and keeping the artist alive. They taught me how good it is to have a friend, and how good it is to be one.

Recent findings suggest that can you tell me about the recurring figure in the prison cell works? You’ve depicted him as a clown. Who does he represent? Who, or what, is the joke?

Industry observers note that the clown keeps coming back in my work. When I look back at everything I made in prison, from beginning to end, I can see that the figures in those first drawings and paintings really were clowns. Over time, all that was left of the clown was the nose and traces of this strange makeup that gradually broke down. The colors started to bleed into one another. I feel that had something to do with how I was changing, how I was growing older in prison. At one point, even the paper tears. I tear it. I don’t know if it was hatred, if I was channeling hatred through my hands, or frustration. I don’t know why it was a clown.

In a recent development, as for the question about the joke, I remember being on hunger strike once, in a group of prisoners that included several men who’d protested on July 11. We’d become friends in there. They were getting sentences of ten years, eight years, five years. It literally seemed like a joke.

To me, the whole thing felt like a circus, like watching a show, only this show had real consequences for people’s lives. So if there’s a joke in it, if there’s an irony, that’s where I see it. They put up this whole circus tent. What happens under it affects so many people’s lives, and none of it makes any sense.What was it like to go years without seeing your whole reflection?

Recent findings suggest that in prison, there was a tiny mirror. Mirrors are prized possessions in there. You hold yours out and someone in another cell, maybe three or six feet away, holds his out too. And there, in that little piece of mirror, you can see the other man’s face. You can see when a guard is coming.

If your mirror is only four inches across, all you ever see of yourself is a piece of your face. You never see your whole body. You go into prison looking one way and come out looking another. The first time I stood in front of a full-length mirror again, it was like coming back to see someone and finding myself face to face with a new person.

I think that found its way into my work. I have a series of self-portraits where my features start to disappear. They’re smudges, scratches, moods. Most of the work I made in prison was like that. I painted states of mind.

It has been revealed that the only portraits that came close to being realistic were the ones I made of my friends. It was all about memory. I wanted to keep existing in my friends’ minds, and I wanted to remember them, too.Two of your works involve faith: a cross, and beside it a pile of idols sinking into an abyss. What is the relationship between your art and faith?

My art has a lot to do with faith and religion. For me, those are two different things. Both are tied to being Cuban. And for as long as I can remember, people have had faith that the system would fall, that the dictatorship would come to an end, that life would get better.

In Cuba, you have very little power to change the reality you live in. There’s no democracy, and the system makes you feel like you can’t fend for yourself. On the island, you’re always waiting for somebody on the outside to save you. And by “save you,” I mean a cousin or a brother sending you money. It’s like having faith in a god who lives somewhere out there, some kind of extraterrestrial being who’s going to keep you going on the island. You put your faith in finding a girlfriend or a boyfriend who has money, or in a foreigner coming along, marrying you and taking you away. The system is so rigid that you have very little room to change your own circumstances.

Before prison, I made performances that drew on images of the Virgin Mary and the saints. What interests me is how these objects change the way people behave, how they shape a culture, and how those in power use them to manipulate people.

Prison is maybe one of the last places where you lose whatever say you still had over your own life. Your future is in the hands of a prosecutor or whoever else gets to decide. It’s like living in a jungle where a lion decides which animal it wants to eat that day, and you pray it won’t be you.

According to recent reports, confinement also brings you face-to-face with yourself. You get in touch with something more visceral in yourself, something more animal. And all you’re left with is the faith that tomorrow might be better.

That reminds me of a story about a friend of mine in prison. He’d been waiting a year or so for his trial, and he was getting desperate. Nothing had been proven against him.

One day he used the five minutes a week they gave him on the phone to call his lawyer. He stated, “Hey, tell me something. Any news?”.

His lawyer said, “Don’t worry. Last night I dreamed they were going to let you go.”.

Industry observers note that in another work, a maze fills the cell. Is it a way out or another kind of trap?

Recent findings suggest that I think the labyrinth has to do with how you feel in prison. When you’re in prison, you really have no way out. But there’s also the question of what you can do with that one small space. You have to turn it into your own amusement park. For me, the labyrinth is about the thousand ways you have to reinvent one space to survive in it.

Sources indicate that there’s also something about getting lost so you can find yourself again, and finding yourself only to get lost again. As time goes by, you get tangled up in nostalgia, in sadness, in forgetting. You feel whole places in your mind starting to disappear, and you find yourself holding on to the memory of them.

According to recent reports, your practice is so community-driven. How did you keep that part of yourself alive in solitary?

The place where I lived was called Pasillo 20, Corridor 20. It was in the maximum-security section at Guanajay, cut off from most of the other prisoners. For five years, I lived among about 20 men.

Some of the men painted or drew. I started what I called the San Isidro Grants. For two or three months, as long as my money lasted, I gave some money to men who painted and bought them materials so they could keep painting. I brought in art history books and gave them away.

I also made work outside the prison while I was still inside. One piece that mattered a lot to me was Momento Cero, which I made with Coco Fusco. People counted down the days I had left in prison. There was also Fe de vida. During the Havana Biennial, we invited curators and artists to come to visit me in prison. Reaching out to people outside was connected to what I was doing with the men I lived with, finding ways to make room for community, kindness and love in a place that was so violent.

You arrived in the United States at a moment when artists here are facing censorship and funding cuts on a scale I haven’t seen in my lifetime. What has it been like to land in this context?

In a recent development, first of all, I feel like I haven’t quite landed here yet. I mean that physically, in my body, but also in my thinking and how I see things as an artist. What I can say is that the little I’ve seen and heard here doesn’t come close to the lack of freedom in Cuba.

Sources indicate that now I’ve come to a country I hope will be a place of passage for me. When you speak from New York, your words carry more legitimacy than if you’re speaking from, say, Havana or Haiti. I don’t know why the world gives that so much weight. Well, yes, I do know why.

Coming here, I can see that this country is going through a transition, a crisis. There’s conflict in the relationships between institutions, art, and artists. I think this is a moment when artists have to take responsibility. We can use art to resist, to change things, and to put forward a vision of a better world.

Do you see any parallels between what you experienced in Cuba and what’s happening here, or do you see them as fundamentally different?

In a recent development, the danger in drawing a parallel is that someone can always say, “Look what happens to people in Cuba. That doesn’t happen to you here. You’ve got me to thank for that, so you have to do what I say.” That’s where populism comes in. If you understand which freedoms an American artist enjoys and what artists elsewhere have to live without, you have a starting point. You can defend the ground you’ve gained and recognize when someone is using those freedoms to blackmail you.

Recent findings suggest that we need to keep those differences in view. That’s how we recognize what we’ve already won as a nation and keep fighting for the freedoms we still need.

How have Cubans on the island and in the diaspora responded to the politics of your release and to your ability to keep making art in prison?

I think my art and the art of my generation, the work of the San Isidro Movement and others, have had an impact on Cuba, both on the island and in the diaspora. It’s only been five years since July 11, 2021, and people already recognize the part that my work, and the art we made together in San Isidro, played in the spirit of rebellion that emerged in 2018, 2019, 2020 and 2021.

For me, those five years in prison are one big work of art, one long performance. I call it “an involuntary artistic gesture.” The dictatorship acts on my body against my will, and what it does to me provokes an aesthetic response in other people.

The other thing that matters is social media and everything that played out there when I arrived in the United States. What struck me was how it exposed some bad habits that have taken hold in the way Cubans use social media. I’m talking about people acting irresponsibly. Some influencers have learned how to make money on YouTube, Facebook and Instagram. Controversy brings in viewers, and viewers bring in money.

What matters most to me is what I’ve experienced walking the streets of Miami. From 99 percent of the people I’ve met, if not 100 percent, what I’ve felt is affection. I’ve felt love.

When you think about what art is for and what an artist owes the world, has your view changed since prison?

I think art is one of the tools we have as human beings to transform society and culture. And when I say culture, I mean it in the broadest sense, right down to the way we behave. Those in power know what art can do. They use it when it serves their interests. When it doesn’t, they go after it. They try to put art itself in prison.

Art is one of the teeth on the gear that keeps society moving. And the artist is the one who thinks, who proposes something, who puts their own body on the line. So, I think the artist bears the greatest responsibility.

An artist’s responsibility extends to humanity as a whole. There’s a commitment to humanism there: understanding that you have power and, more than that, a responsibility. Because if you don’t use your art to help people, someone else will use it for purposes that don’t help them.

When you picture your studio, or your next show, a year from now, what do you see?

It has been revealed that A year from now, I’d love the work I brought out of Guanajay to have found homes in archives, museums and private collections. I want someone standing there to get a sense of what one human being lived through in confinement. I was a Cuban in prison. I was also a human being locked up. Someone in a prison anywhere in the world could go through what I went through, you know? For my studio, what I want is room to work and room to try things. There are sculptures I want to propose, ideas I couldn’t develop in Cuba because of the repression.

I also hope I’ll have helped more Americans understand something about Cuba. Our two peoples are so close, yet there’s still a romantic view of Cuba here, and that has consequences for us Cubans. Fidel Castro was a dictator. We’ve lived under a dictatorship for more than 60 years.

In a recent development, more than anything, I’d like people in the arts here to understand our work and make room for it in the stories and images that are part of everyday American life. What happens on that island finds echoes in so many other places.

Recent findings suggest that the Bayeux Tapestry is the gift that keeps on giving. UK museums such as Reading Museum and the Great North Museum: Hancock are experiencing a “Bayeux bounce,” according to the Museums Association.

Replicas of the scroll-like panel of linen cloth, which measures at 230 feet long and is populated with 58 scenes, are driving visitors to museums other than the British Museum, where the tapestry is on loan until July next year. Tickets to the British Museum’s presentation have been sold out numerous times. Related Articles Bayeux Tapestry Display to Change Upon Return to Normandy Next Year George Osborne Personally Helped Secure Controversial $6.6 M. British Museum Sponsorship, Emails Show.

It has been revealed that reading Museum’s museum manager, Matthew Williams, mentioned that the museum’s Victorian replica of the Bayeux Tapestry has driven a 74 percent increase in footfall since October, with 16,693 visitors. The tapestry at Reading Museum is free to visit, and photography is allowed, unlike at the British Museum, where the tapestry is ticketed at £33 and photography is banned in order to control the long queues.

“We have trained more staff to deliver our public tours and recruited more welcome volunteers to help us manage the crowds, especially at weekends and school holidays,” said Williams. “We have made sure to keep our website updated to manage expectations and to clearly show when the [replica] Bayeux Tapestry is closed for booked tours or when it will be busy, to avoid disappointment.”.

The Bayeux Tapestry replica has resulted in optimistic numbers for the museum, with tours booked until June 2027, the cafe’s income up by 46 percent, donations increased by 83 percent, and shop sales soaring by 93 percent.

The copy of the Bayeux Tapestry at the Great North Museum: Hancock is on display until January 17, 2027, and is made out of paper, stretching approximately 16 feet longer than the original. The museum has experienced a 23 percent increase in visitors this October, with 3,107 more visitors than last year, while donations have climbed 30 percent, retail up 13 percent and the cafe hopping by 11 percent.

In a recent development, other museums are taking advantage of the Bayeux Tapestry replica. The Nicholson Institute in Staffordshire will display its own copy from January 12 to March 31, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

In a recent development, future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?".

Recent findings suggest that future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:.

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:.

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610.

The table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:.

FV = PMT x [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r].

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

Industry observers note that A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Recent findings suggest that every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:.

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

The Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:.

According to recent reports, this works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

It has been revealed that the FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:.

In a recent development, the table shows how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Recent findings suggest that when projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

In a recent development, add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

It has been revealed that test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

It has been revealed that for long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

In a recent development, the Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

Recent findings suggest that in tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Recent findings suggest that future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

Recent findings suggest that the volume comes from the holdings of the widely respected American collector Mickey Cartin. Christie’s is offering up to $8 million worth of selections from his collection, ranging from Netherlandish painting to contemporary art and, of course, rare books. Upward of 80 objects will be spread over more than 10 auctions in London, Paris, and New York, from this November until July 2027.

According to recent reports, the Book of Miracles was completed in the city of Augsburg around 1552. Its geographical origins are known because some of the captions refer to events “here in Augsburg,” and the paper bears watermarks associated with that city and time period. The makers are thought to be Hans Burgkmair the Younger, Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, and their respective workshops. Its imagery, says the auction house, draws on the work of some of the best-known artists of the German Renaissance, such as Albrecht Dürer and Hans Holbein the Younger.

Industry observers note that the book begins with the Creation described in the Christian Bible and moves chronologically through other events in that book as well as ancient and medieval history, and finally, the Apocalypse. Events that were relatively newsy at the time appear, including a celestial phenomenon observed from Augsburg in 1541 and a hailstorm in Dordrecht in 1552.

The book traces back to a private collection in Bavaria. Munich bookseller and auctioneer Hugo Ruef, describing it as coming from the library of a small South German Baroque castle, sold it in 2008 for €127,500 ($140,305 at today’s rate of exchange). By 2010, it was with London dealer James Faber, who specializes in European drawings, and then it went to Cartin.

Industry observers note that “The Book of Miracles is an extraordinary window onto the Renaissance imagination,” said Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, in press materials. “Its 167 miniatures capture a world fascinated by signs, wonders and unexplained phenomena, bringing together comets, eclipses, floods, monstrous births and visions of the Apocalypse. What makes the manuscript particularly compelling is the way it sits between observation and belief: these images record real events and natural phenomena, while also revealing how people in the 16th century sought to understand what they were seeing and what these extraordinary occurrences might signify.”.

As the New York Review of Books noted in 2014, on the occasion of a new facsimile printing by Taschen, the 16th-century book came as part of a “boom” in compendia of miracles that grew out of a new focus on reading the Bible, and wrote that in it, “One astonishing, delicious, supersaturated picture follows another.” Apollo fittingly described the book as “a revelation,” notes Taschen.
