Breaking: Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year winner named

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.
  • The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.
  • Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The wayfinding scheme for London‘s V&A East Storehouse has won Dezeen Awards 2026 design project of the year following the announcement of all 16 design category winners at a party in London.

The 16 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme include designs by Laurids Gallée and John Tree, as well as Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphic identity for the V&A East Storehouse experience won the design project of the year award and was also named graphic design of the year.

V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

The master jury cited the project as a “sophisticated wayfinding scheme that demonstrates how signage can do far more than direct: it can define identity, shape experience and establish a sense of place”.

The judges praised the design for its “clarity, confidence and restraint, seamlessly guiding visitors through the V&A East Storehouse while adding to the character of the building”.

V&A East Storehouse was up against designs that included a constellation of gloopy-looking polished resin lights, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van and a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

Read more about all the winning design projects below:.

Design project of the year and graphic design of the year: V&A East Storehouse by Fieldwork Facility.

Design studio Fieldwork Facility was challenged with navigating visitors to the V&A’s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse.

The Hackney design studio looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse: Gen-Z apps and services.

“This fun and informative signage and wayfinding perfectly embraces the changing nature of the V&A East Storehouse,” remarked the master jury.

“As the displays change, the signage, captions and general wayfinding can be updated efficiently, embracing the adaptability and lack of formality of the museum.”.

Furniture design of the year: Dado Series by Allen Kaufmann Objects.

Berlin studio Allen Kaufmann Architekten won furniture design of the year for its Dado series of tables and shelves.

What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial.

The practice adapted a traditional woodworking joint to create a flat-pack range that can be assembled completely without tools nor glue, screws, brackets or other fasteners.

Recent findings suggest that “What is simple in appearance is underscored with a well-resolved and detailed construction made from a monomaterial,” the judges noted. “The shelving is satisfying to assemble and demonstrates everything furniture needs to be, and no more.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Seating design of the year: Kino by Pablo Castillo Design.

Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo won seating design of the year for Kino, a cantilevered 3D-printed chair for Decibel.

Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

In a recent development, its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

“The 3D printing of furniture is becoming more refined and this is a strong example of that,” said the master jury.

Industry observers note that “The mono-material construction is sophisticated and has a strong aesthetic profile,” they continued. “Modern shapes meet zero-waste manufacturing; surely the future.”.

Collectible design of the year: Lima Charlie by Studio Laurids Gallée.

Austrian designer Laurids Gallée won collectible design of the year for Lima Charlie, a series of five colourful, sculptural lamps.

Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship.

The lighting collection comprises five hand-cast resin light works and machined aluminium pieces.

It has been revealed that first, the designer used digital processes to determine each composition. Then, casting solid blocks of the material before colouring, cutting and sculpting them into shape. Each piece was meticulously sanded and polished to arrive at the desired smooth surface.

According to recent reports, “Mesmerising, intriguing and evocative, these lights are truly original and demonstrate a high level of care in their meticulous craftsmanship,” praised the judges. “Beautiful treasures to enhance any space.”.

Bespoke design of the year: Real Time Schiphol People’s Clock by Maarten Baas.

Dutch designer Maarten Baas won bespoke design of the year for The People’s Clock, a choreographed representation of the passage of time at Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.

It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.

Baas recruited 1,000 participants – the majority being airport employees – to form the hands of The People’s Clock and move in sync, forming the hour and minute hands. The second hand comprises a single person running a lap of the circular perimeter each minute.

“This timepiece in Amsterdam’s busy airport momentarily takes users away from the efficient functionality of the space by providing a reference to the time in a more playful and poetic way,” said the master jury.

“It was an ambitious undertaking to make the piece, which celebrates and gives ownership to the airport workers.”.

Lighting design of the year: Hoop Table Lamp by John Tree for Vaarnii.

Designer John Tree won lighting design of the year for the Hoop Table Lamp for Finnish brand Vaarni.

There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.

The monolithic light combines a block of solid pine wood – synonymous with the Finnish brand’s designs – with a hooped shade of thin pine veneer, sourced from a sustainably managed forest.

“We were all drawn to the simple and characterful gestures of this table lamp, which embraces warmth from a common timber,” the judges mentioned.

“There is a confidence in the minimal use of materials and a cuteness in the ensuing form.”.

Architectural lighting design of the year: Cologne Cathedral by Licht Kunst Licht.

Lighting design studio Licht Kunst Licht won architectural lighting design of the year for its illumination of Cologne Cathedral’s historic facade.

This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline.

The lighting scheme used more than 700 surface-mounted LED luminaires to transform nighttime views of the world’s tallest cathedral without drilling a single hole in its delicate stonework.

“This well-considered lighting scheme successfully highlights Cologne’s monumental cathedral as a jewel on the night skyline,” the judges praised.

“The light sources are subtly integrated and have managed to reduce energy consumption while creating maximum impact for this city landmark,” they added.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Surface design of the year: Basic Third by Pretty Plastic.

Dutch manufacturer Pretty Plastic won surface design of the year for its Basic Third tiles.

There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.

The cladding material was developed by the Pretty Plastic manufacturer, started by architecture studios Overtreders W and Bureau SLA.

The tiles, which were made from 30,987 kilograms of post-consumer plastic waste, have been applied as cladding for Plus Ultra III, the first timber laboratory building in the Netherlands.

“Pretty Plastics has chosen to work with the worst kind of plastic – PVC – and found a way to repurpose the material into tiles,” stated the judges.

“The material is already fire-compliant and UV stable, making it a worthy contender for the cladding of buildings,” they continued. “There is an inherent beauty and honesty to the product, adding texture and depth to the architecture.”.

Looking ahead, the judges remarked “its impact will be proven by how easy it is to scale.”.

Textile design of the year: Bianni Wool Paper by Arudeko.

Mexican design studio won textile design of the year for Bianni, a paper-like material made from colourful waste wool.

With so much wool waste in the world, this new material adds value to the waste.

Sourced from the off-cuts of handmade carpets and cushions crafted by local weaving communities in Teotitlán del Valle, Mexico, Arudeko saw the potential to use the surplus material and save it from being discarded.

Bianni can be sculpted into everything from lampshades to room dividers.

“With so much wool waste in the world, this latest material adds value to the waste,” the judges commended.

Industry observers note that “Furthermore, the processing provides employment to skilled locals, the outcome being an interesting and beautiful paper alternative to be applied to other products,” they said. “There is much potential for further exploration across the world.”.

Workplace design of the year: Area by Foster + Partners and Kettal.

Foster + Partners and Kettal won workplace design of the year for their modular Area table system.

There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition.

According to recent reports, designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power. The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

“There is an appealing monumentalism to this office desk and a tactility in the simplicity and richness of the material composition,” said the judges.

“There are sophisticated elements and thoughtful hidden details for integrating technology into an otherwise minimalist design,” they continued.

Product design (consumer design) of the year: Pedal 4 by Minimal.

British start-up Minimal won product design (consumer design) of the year for Pedal 4, an electric cargo bike with the carrying capacity of a small van.

A smart latest vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries.

The four-wheeled, pedal-assist cargo vehicle was built to take up less room on the roads and evade traffic even on London’s crowded and complex streets. It is now operating in London with delivery companies Royal Mail and Evri.

“A smart newly introduced vehicle typology that addresses the challenges of inner city deliveries,” praised the judges.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a great ‘last mile’ replacement for large polluting vans. The slender design manoeuvres easily in city streets while the electric motor emits no noxious pollutants,” they continued.

“The vehicles’ local assembly also allows it to be easily repaired.”.

Product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year: CurifyLabs PharmaPrinter Aurum by Studio Aslak Siimes.

Industrial design firm Studio Aslak Siimes and Finnish startup CurifyLabs won product design (health, wellbeing and wearables) of the year for pharmaceutical compounding system, PharmaPrinter Aurum.

It’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered.

The system is designed to improve the process of creating patient-specific medicine, born from the realisation that almost 30 per cent of all medication requires personalisation rather than being mass-manufactured, according to studio founder Aslak Siimes.

It has been revealed that “This device offers a real innovation in precision healthcare and decentralises the production of pills,” the judges said. “Precise medical doses are prepared bespoke for each customer, reducing waste and eliminating human error.”.

“Furthermore, it’s refreshing to see something so functional having also been aesthetically considered,” they added.

Product design (bathroom) of the year: Dekoda by Kohler Health.

Kohler Health won product design (bathroom) of the year for Dekoda, a health tracker specifically for the toilet.

This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions.

Designed to be discreet and intuitive, the tracker clips to the side of the toilet bowl to give insights on gut health and hydration levels, and to detect the presence of blood.

Sources indicate that “This is an innovative, early-diagnostic device for ongoing monitoring of health conditions,” the judges remarked. “The design of the device is discreet and visually passive, making it suitable for its function in the bathroom.”.

Installation design of the year: Einder for USB002 Tour by Boris Acket and Fred Again.

Visual artist Boris Acket won installation design of the year for Einder, which featured as the standout show design for DJ Fred again..’s USB002 Tour.

Industry observers note that this lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!

The installation features a large suspended sheet of fabric which floats above the audience like a transparent, breathing roof.

Throughout the concert, the sculpture wafts and moves across the audience, creating smaller and larger spaces, static spatial gestures, storms, and water surfaces.

The judges summed up the project as “stunning, emotive, immersive, dynamic, simple”.

In a recent development, “This lightweight and flexible installation uses minimum material to maximum effect, making it evocative while sustainable. More please!”.

Sustainable design of the year: Datecrete by Datecrete Studio.

Architect Sara Abu Farha and engineer Khaled Shalka won sustainable design of the year for Datecrete, a concrete-style material developed by Abu Farha and Shalka formed from crushed dates.

This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete.

The project aims to demonstrate how the abundant regional byproduct can become part of an architectural material language. Patent-pending, Datecrete can be produced as floor and wall tiles, cladding, furniture, lighting elements and smaller design objects.

“This is a necessary regional innovation, repurposing an abundant waste material (date pits) into a local construction material, and providing a welcome alternative to concrete,” mentioned the master jury.

“The processing of the pits is decentralised, so it has the potential to scale in communities across the date-growing region.”.

Material innovation of the year: Mimmik Tile by Front.

Dutch sustainability platform Front and biotechnology company Biomason won material innovation of the year for Mimmik, a low-carbon, concrete-like floor tile strengthened by bacteria.

This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete.

Front believes Mimmik is the first bacteria-grown tile to be industrially produced, making a sustainable technology available to a wide market of specifiers looking to reduce the carbon footprint of their commercial projects.

“This tile design is genuinely pushing innovation forward in its creation; collaborating with bacteria as a sustainable alternative to concrete,” praised the judges.

According to recent reports, “As such, the embodied carbon is greatly reduced,” they noted. “The production is scalable and could shift the dial in the future production of tiles and paving.”.

#9766. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1717 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone.
  • There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

Recent findings suggest that if you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

According to recent reports, “The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”.

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

According to recent reports, the textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

It has been revealed that some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

According to recent reports, all things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

It has been revealed that regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Sources indicate that because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, says Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin states. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”.

In a recent development, that’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health concerns.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Industry observers note that over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra notes, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

It has been revealed that because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar claims. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that as researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

This article is part of our latest Opinion section, a format for argument-driven essays on critical questions shaping our field.

In a recent development, in 2022, Tokyo's Nakagin Capsule Tower was demolished, bringing an end to one of modern architecture's most recognizable experiments in adaptability. Designed by Kisho Kurokawa and completed in 1972, the building consisted of 140 prefabricated capsules attached to two concrete cores. Its architectural proposition was radical: individual capsules could be replaced as needs evolved, allowing the building to renew itself without dismantling its principal structure. Yet over five decades, the proposed replacement system was never realized. Despite various preservation efforts, deteriorating building services and difficulties in collective decision-making eventually led to its demolition.

Tech Report: Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year announced

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.
  • The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.
  • Recent findings suggest that la Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An old sailor’s home that pays homage to its nautical heritage has won Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors project of the year following the announcement of all 14 interiors category winners at a party in London.

The 14 winners awarded in Dezeen’s annual awards programme are located in 10 different countries, including Australia, China, Czech Republic, Kazakhstan, Mexico and Ukraine.

Recent findings suggest that la Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects won the interiors project of the year award, sponsored by Gaggenau. It was also named residential interior (small) project of the year.

“This was probably the boldest and most well-executed project we saw,” remarked the judges.

“They kept everything that was already there and made a much more interesting place,” adding that, “it’s very well-thought-out in terms of how space has been used.”.

La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners, including a restaurant that features “direct and unrefined” materials to create tactile interior in Canada, a pink stepped-facade-fronted commercial building and interiors in Mexico and a boutique that recalls a traditional yurt in Kazakhstan.

A boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture and a warehouse into a workspace divided by glass partitions and filled with design classics, including an entire Jean Prouvé house were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning interiors projects below:.

Interiors project of the year and residential interior (small) of the year: La Casa del Pirata by Raul Sanchez Architects.

The Spanish practice renovated the home in Mataro, Spain, which belonged to a sailor in the 19th century, updating its interiors to suit the lifestyle of his descendant, who lives there now.

There was no discussion – this was the winner.

The project saw the renovation of three spaces: the entrance hall, the dining room and the living area. The judges praised the project’s bold approach, noting there was no deliberation over its winning credentials: “There was no discussion – this was the winner.”.

“It’s super unusual,” they continued, “and we liked to see an intervention in a very historical space where they decided to not play it safe.”.

Residential interior (large) of the year: Garden Home by Gisbert Pöppler.

Local studio Gisbert Pöppler won residential interior (large) of the year for its renovation of a 1920s villa in Ruhr, Germany.

For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior.

The interior design features a bold colour scheme and artisanal details that reflect its association with the Deutscher Werkbund movement, which caught the judges’ eyes.

“For this project, we were swayed by the colours and use of materials, as well as the contrast between the very classic exterior of the house and its interior,” they remarked.

“It has character and doesn’t play it safe,” they continued.

Restaurant interior of the year: Jeju by &Daughters.

Canadian studio &Daughters won restaurant interior of the year for Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver, Canada.

This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element.

A rich material palette of basalt, cork, concrete, thatch and wood characterises the restaurant interior, which nods to traditional touches in its contemporary design.

Industry observers note that “This project has a level of innovation while being quite exquisite in every element,” the master jury said. “It’s contemporary and still a bit traditional. There’s also a cultural influence that’s being used well and isn’t just there for decoration.”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Bar and cafe interior of the year: Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design.

Laibei 1087 by Tant A Temps Design in Xi’an, China, won bar and cafe interior of the year, sponsored by Programa.

There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.

Located inside the Beilin Museum, the cafe’s interior aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty and used a minimal intervention renovation strategy with every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

“This project is newly introduced and modern, but still connected to the past,” the judges remarked.

“There are a lot of beautiful projects, but this one is really refreshing – it’s working with the building, but also reinventing it.”.

“The architect has taken symbolic elements and simplified them, which makes it feel quite fresh.”.

Hotel and short-stay interior of the year: Moon Gang by YSG Studio.

Australian studio YSG won hotel and short-stay interior of the year for its conversion of a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali, Indonesia.

There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit.

Focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture, Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

YSG was influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“There’s a lot of innovation and playfulness here, and a good use of local craftsmanship, as well as a collaborative spirit,” commended the master jury.

Workplace interior (small) of the year: Rosadoce by Reims 502.

Rosadoce by Reims 502 in Querétaro, Mexico won workplace interior (small) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior.

Featuring a stepped facade, the commercial building’s pink characterises the warm feel of the interior, being used throughout the workplace with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone.

“This is a very architectural project, but that architecture has influenced the interior,” noted the master jury.

“We like how they connected the interior and exterior design,” they continued, “it’s an adaptable and very sophisticated design.”.

Workplace interior (large) of the year: Not A Hotel Office by Not A Hotel.

Not a Hotel’s own office in Tokyo, Japan won workplace interior (large) of the year, sponsored by Framery.

We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic.

The Japanese hospitality company’s in-house architecture team turned a 1967 warehouse into a workspace featuring a brutalist design divided by glass partitions and a spacious interior with seven-metre-tall ceilings.

“We found this one very impressive; it was quite radical and dramatic,” noted the judges.

“It really makes coming to the office feel like a dip back into the culture.”.

Retail interior (small) of the year: Gunia Project Showroom by Temp Project.

Local studio Temp Project won retail interior (small) of the year for its lifestyle store in Kyiv, Ukraine.

The mix between the old and fresh is very interesting.

Modern materials, including mirrors and tiled surfaces, were used to complement the building’s original ornate interior for brand Gunia Project, which occupies the ground floor of a late 19th-century building located on a historic street near Kyiv’s Golden Gate.

“The mix between the old and fresh is very interesting,” remarked the judges.

“It must have been a constraining space to work in,” they observed, “but the end result feels very carefully edited and sophisticated.”.

Retail interior (large) of the year: Messa House by Up2date.

Up2date Architects won retail interior (large) of the year for the minimalist Messa House store in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect.

Commissioned for womenswear brand Messa, the 350-square-metre store was designed to reimagine the form of a Kazakh yurt, with breakout areas and an on-site cafe.

“Beige interiors are boring unless they’re done well and for this one, the use of material is just perfect,” praised the master jury.

The judges also commended “the contrast between the glossy tiles, wall and furniture”.

“It’s like a small architectural world inside the space,” they stated.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Leisure and wellness interior of the year: Unravel by Atelier Write.

Japanese studio Atelier Write won the leisure and wellness interior of the year for its hair salon project in Tokyo, Japan.

This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there.

Named Unravel, the project transformed a warehouse with statement features such as suspending mirrors, shelves and curtains from a series of industrial rails that allow the entire space to be reconfigured.

“This is a really good use of space – it’s very clever how they have integrated something that you wouldn’t imagine would fit in there,” remarked the judges.

“It’s an innovative, moveable space and the movement has purpose; it’s not just a gimmick.”.

Exhibition design (interior) of the year: Life Behind the Walls by B² Architecture.

B2 Architecture won exhibition design (interior) of the year for its Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, Czech Republic.

They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way.

Using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea, the 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

“In this project, the colours black, white and red are used really well in a graphical way,” said the master jury.

The judges also noted its material sensitivity, noting how surprising “the designers use soft materials to create emotions,” adding that “there’s a contrast between the technology and the use of textiles”.

“They have used the materials that everyone uses for exhibition design, but in a new way,” they added.

Kitchen interior of the year: Pine Island Cottage by Thom Fougere Studio & Bureau Tempo.

Canadian studios Bureau Tempo and Thom Fougere won kitchen interior of the year for Pine Island Cottage in Ontario, Canada.

You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.

The getaway retreat’s materials are informed by the rocky surroundings of the host island in Ontario’s Georgian Bay.

“This kitchen is very functional and well laid out, but it’s also super beautiful and we like that they used local materials,” remarked the master jury.

“You can imagine being there – washing the dishes with that view, you’d actually want to do them.”.

Bathroom interior of the year: Lumeah by Pepper & Well.

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well won bathroom interior of the year for Lumeah in Macedon, Australia.

We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass.

The studio took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing the fresh en-suite within one of the most intact examples of residential work by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

“We really liked the use of materials in this bathroom, with its mix of concrete, stone and glass,” mentioned the judges.

“The studio did a good job of creating a contemporary interior in a historic building, and we enjoyed how the bathroom feels like it continues out into the garden.”.

Sustainable interior of the year: Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo Design Studio.

Chinese studio RooMoo won sustainable interior of the year for Cloudhaus Hotel in Chongqing, China.

This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins were repurposed for the 24-room retreat for its renovation, which the judges noted for being well-documented.

“This is a great effort and if you want to be sustainable, it’s really well done,” the master jury said.

“They took a dark, concrete space and turned it into a warm interior through the use of wood, while keeping a lot of the existing materials,” they continued.

Recent findings suggest that weightlifting isn’t the only way to build muscle. Rucking, or walking with a weighted backpack, is also highly effective. It’s easy to start, can be done anywhere, and helps build muscle, burn fat, and boost endurance.

In a recent development, curious? Keep reading to discover why rucking might become your newly introduced favorite workout!

It has been revealed that rucking is like taking your regular walk and cranking up the intensity with heavy cargo. It’s as simple as strapping on a weighted backpack (aka rucksack) and hitting the pavement, the trail, or wherever you like to roam. Originally dreamed up by the military to toughen up soldiers, rucking, or a rucksack march has, er, marched into civilian life as a killer workout.

What makes it awesome? The extra weight transforms a casual stroll into a workout that means business. Plus, it’s customizable — you can load up as much or as little weight as you want, making it perfect for any fitness level. And the best part is that you can ruck just about anywhere.

Rucking isn’t just a walk in the park — it’s a powerful workout that packs a punch in all the right places. Here’s why rucking deserves a spot in your fitness routine:.

Think of rucking as the ultimate multitasker for your body. It’s like lifting weights but with cardio to keep your heart pumping.

As you lug that weighted backpack around, your legs, back, and core are putting in serious work, building strength, and endurance with every (weighted) step.

Recent findings suggest that want to torch calories without the treadmill monotony? Rucking’s got you covered. The extra weight and steady movement combo turns your stroll into a calorie-burning machine. Perfect for shedding any additional pounds while keeping things interesting.

Carrying a weighted backpack helps your posture. Your core has to stay engaged to keep you balanced, which helps align your body and ward off injury.

If you’ve had a baby, rucking can be a game-changer, helping combat the postural shifts of pregnancy and hauling around kids. Plus, it builds the functional strength you need for everyday life, like lifting groceries or wrangling toddlers.

Rucking easily fits into a busy schedule. You don’t need special equipment beyond a sturdy backpack or a gym membership, and you can do it while multitasking — think walking the dog in the morning or pushing a stroller. Plus, the whole family can join in, making it a great way to combine fitness with family time.

Starting rucking is easy, but here are some tips to help you get the most out of your rucks:.

Rucking is generally safe, but here’s how to stay injury-free:.

According to recent reports, yes, rucking can help build muscle, especially in your legs, core, and back. The added weight provides resistance, similar to strength training.

Start with 10 to 15% of your body weight and adjust based on your comfort and fitness level. Heavier weights can affect your balance and stance, making injuries more likely. As you progress, you can gradually increase the weight.

Yes. Rucking forces your upper back and shoulder muscles to step up, giving your traps a solid workout as you carry the weight.

Industry observers note that ruck yes! Rucking is a low-impact, full-body workout that kicks butt.

It has been revealed that tell your boring walk on the treadmill to ruck off and trade it in for a waltz about with a weighted rucksack. Rucking could be the secret sauce your fitness routine has been missing, helping you build muscle, shed pounds, or get those steps in.

#9759. Cycling Metrics Guide: What to Measure for Better Rides

📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3563 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Cycling Metrics Guide: What to Measure for Better Rides

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that my favorite metric has always been feel.
  • Sources indicate that that noted, there have certainly been races where I’ve blown up—where the implosion probably could have been prevented had I been watching my watts.
  • Today, I strike a compromise between luddite and tech-geek, tracking my resting heart rate and heart rate variability with an Oura ring, and recording heart rate for most rides so I can keep an eye on how fatigued and/or fresh I am.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that my favorite metric has always been feel. I trained for two Ironman, including World Championships in Kona and entire mountain bike stage races like Cape Epic and Brasil Ride tracking nothing but time, distance, speed, and how I felt. I’d trained enough with heart rate and power to know how they worked, but I always reverted to feel.

Sources indicate that that noted, there have certainly been races where I’ve blown up—where the implosion probably could have been prevented had I been watching my watts. And the times I did spend training with power, there’s little question my sessions were more precise and likely more productive. It can be easier to stay on track with training when you have measurable goals and quantifiable sessions.

Today, I strike a compromise between luddite and tech-geek, tracking my resting heart rate and heart rate variability with an Oura ring, and recording heart rate for most rides so I can keep an eye on how fatigued and/or fresh I am.

Sources indicate that ultimately, I think that’s the best process when it comes to using data. Start with the basics, then add on as you get more experience. Most riders end up settling on a handful of metrics they rely on most.

Here, a primer to get you started tracking your cycling metrics.

In a recent development, obviously, tracking cycling metrics generally means you need a device to capture that data. Most of the metrics, such as speed, distance, time, and elevation, mentioned here can be captured with a GPS-enabled bike computer like a Garmin, Wahoo, Lezyne, or Hammerhead. The deeper you want to dive into the data, the more sensors you need.

Great for: The satisfaction of seeing your pace pick up.

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer.

Your miles per hour (or kilometers per hour, depending on where you live) is a fun metric to track, and it can tell you broadly high much fitter you’re getting. The catch: It’s not very reliable to use in training because so many factors influence it. For example, you may be cranking out World Pro-level wattage but if you’re doing so into a 30-mph block headwind, you’re not going to be setting any land speed records.

Your average speed is best used as an indicator of how your training is going overtime: If you are now consistently averaging 16+ mph on a loop that you used to average 15+ mph, you can see you’re getting fitter and faster.

You can track your average time with and without your stopping time factored into the pace. Most people don’t factor stoppage (or “café time”) in because they want to see moving time only. But if you’re training for a big event like a gravel race, it’s important to know your average speed including that stoppage time, because races often set cut offs based on a 10-mph pace, which includes rest stops. Once you see how long those “short breaks” really are, you can learn to keep them quick and avoid missing time cuts. You’ll also know how fast you need to ride to allow yourself the stoppage time you plan to take.

Great for: Watching your endurance increase.

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer.

We all like to see how far we’ve gone, especially on a big ride. Distance can be a motivational metric to track. If you’re averaging 50 to 80 miles a week, can you make it 100? Can you set an annual goal of hitting 5,000 miles or more? When tracking distance, it’s important to take into consideration what type of riding you do. Riding 60 miles on flat roads is very different from 60 miles of singletrack. One might take three to four hours while the other takes the better part of a day.

According to recent reports, distance is also important to track if you’re training for a ride of a specific distance. If you want to ride a century in the fall, you’ll want to work up to it by hitting 50-mile and 75-mile rides as the event approaches.

Great for: Learning pacing for eventsEquipment needed: Any watch will do, but a bike computer can automatically track moving time and stoppage time.

Most cyclists train by time because that’s our most finite resource. How much time you have each week to ride determines how to best use that time if your goal is to improve performance. Riders with a tight time budget are best served doing polarized training that emphasizes short, hard interval workouts during the week and longer rides as time permits on the weekend.

Great for: Bragging rights and building strength (hills make you stronger!).

Equipment needed: A GPS enabled bike computer.

Elevation gain in cycling is the total amount of feet (or meters) you climb over the course of a ride. Climbing is good training, because your body must work harder in the effort to overcome the pull of gravity. If you’re the kind of rider who routinely avoids inclines, setting climbing goals and tracking elevation can give your cycling fitness a boost. If your goal is to focus on elevations, start by aiming to hit an average of 500 feet per 10 miles. Work up to what some climbing lovers call the “golden ratio” of 1,000 feet of vertical gain per 10 miles of riding.

Great for: Fine-tuning your fueling.

Equipment needed: Apps like Strava will estimate your calorie burn, but for more accurate data, use a heart rate monitor and/or power meter.

A calorie is a unit of energy provided by food. The calorie metric provided on your cycling computer or smartwatch is how many of those units you used to complete your ride. But calorie calculations are an imperfect science.

Sources indicate that some devices will provide estimates based on algorithms, which are just that—estimates. Past research has shown that devices can have a wide margin of error: A Stanford study published in 2017 reported that not one of the seven devices they tested—including the Apple Watch, Fitbit Surge, Mio Alpha 2, Basis Peak, Microsoft Band, PulseOn, and the Samsung Gear S2—delivered an accurate number for calories burned. The most accurate one, the Apple Watch, was off by 27 percent. The least accurate one? Off by 93 percent.

A more recent meta-analysis published in The British Journal of Sports Medicine echoed these findings, indicating that though devices that measure your heart rate along with your movement are more accurate, they all have a pretty significant margin of error.

It has been revealed that apps like GarminConnect, Strava, and other training apps might be a bit better, but they’re not perfect, either, and the number they give you depends heavily on the information you give the app. The more detailed data you input about yourself, such as age, height, weight, gender, and max heart rate, the more accurately their internal algorithms can calculate your calorie burn. Wearing a chest-based heart rate monitor that is synced to your device also helps make your calorie count more accurate.

Ultimately, the best way to know how many calories you burn on a ride is by using a power meter. Power meters measure the work you’re performing and display it in kilojoules, which is a unit of work that takes into account that the human body isn’t 100-percent efficient when turning energy from your fuel stores into physical work, like pedaling a bike.

Recent findings suggest that “Kilojoules and calories burned in cycling convert to a 1:1 ratio,” explains USA Cycling elite coach Daniel Matheny, head coach at Matheny Endurance in Colorado Springs. If your ride file claims you performed 800 kJ of work, you can feel confident within a 5-percent margin of error that you burned about 800 calories.

Tracking calories is useful for helping you fuel for rides. Some riders underestimate the number of calories they’ll burn on a three-hour group ride and end up falling off the back on the verge of bonking three quarters of the way through. Properly fueled riders ride faster and happier.

Just note that the goal is not to replace every calorie you’re burning as you ride. Your gut can’t take that. “Replace about half the calories you’re burning per hour for rides lasting longer than three or four hours to keep fuel levels topped off,” indicates sports physiologist and SkratchLabs founder Allen Lim, Ph.D.

You may also notice that the fitter you become, the fewer calories you burn on a given ride at a given pace. That’s because your body has become more efficient at using oxygen.

Great for: Training leg strength and speed; watching fitness improve for upcoming riders.

Equipment needed: A cycling computer and cadence sensor.

It has been revealed that cadence is the number of revolutions you spin per minute as you pedal. If you have a cadence sensor you can watch your cadence in real time on your bike computer and track your average cadence for each ride.

It has been revealed that it’s debatable how useful it is to track and/or train cadence. Coaches used to recommend athletes aim to pedal 90 rpm, but research doesn’t really show benefits from forcing yourself to do so. In 2019, a team of British researchers found that not only did amateur riders not get any added benefit from high cadence cycling, but they also became less efficient, so they were wasting energy.

Hunter Allen, CEO of Peaks Coaching Group, and author of Training and Racing with a Power Meter explains that your cadence will be determined by two things: your main muscle fiber type and your level of cardiovascular cycling fitness. The balance of those factors (which, of course, can change over time) determine your ideal cadence.

It has been revealed that newer riders tend to pedal more slowly because their cardiovascular system can’t handle the higher heart rate that comes with high cadences. As fitness improves, cadence generally rises.

While you probably don’t need to track your cadence from ride to ride, if you have a cadence sensor, it can help you do cadence drills, such as low gear/high cadence and high gear/low cadence drills that can help build cardiovascular fitness, leg speed, and leg strength.

Great for: Learning what sustainable (and unsustainable) efforts feel like and tracking fitness improvement.

Equipment needed: Your heart, lungs, legs, and brain.

According to recent reports, it doesn’t get any more basic than RPE, your rate of perceived exertion. Put more simply, it's a measure of how hard you feel like you’re working. On a 1 to 10 scale, 1 is coasting along on a flat road with a tailwind, and 10 is full gas, willing yourself not to vomit.

It has been revealed that you can also think of this as your “breath analyzer,” because a monitoring your breathing is an easy way to rate your efforts. Your muscles use more oxygen the harder you push, so breathing rate is a direct indication of work. If you’re able to sing and recite poetry, you’re not working very hard. If you’re gasping uncontrollably, you are maxed out.

According to recent reports, research reveals RPE works just as well as any scientific equipment for measuring your actual effort at any given time, but it doesn’t tell you much more. For instance, you may be huffing and puffing and battling burning legs, but barely producing any power; or you could be feeling chainless while cranking out major wattage. Though you can train by “feel” alone, you get a more complete picture of your daily sessions and progress if you pair it with other metrics like heart rate or power.

It also takes discipline to train by feel because you have to remain tuned in, and it’s all too easy to slack off when you should be pushing or push too hard on a recovery day.

Great for: Creating specific training zones and tuning into your freshness and/or fatigue.

Equipment needed: A heart rate monitor and compatible bike computer or watch.

In a recent development, as your effort increases, your heart pumps more oxygen and nutrient-rich blood to fuel your muscles. The result: Your heart rate goes up. Monitoring your heart beats per minute (BPM) with a heart rate monitor will tell you just how hard you’re working.

Industry observers note that to use heart rate, you need to first determine your max heart rate (MHR)—or the highest number of BPM you can hit. Forget the generic 220 minus your age formula for determining max heart rate and take a field test instead:.

Warm up thoroughly, then do a 10-minute time trial as hard as possible, kicking it into full throttle for the final 60 seconds, aiming to full on sprint the final 20 seconds. Cool down and check your data for MHR. Repeat two more times (with rest days in between) to find your true max. Once you have your max, you can break down various levels of training efforts according to percentages of that number. As you get fitter, you’ll be able to ride faster at lower heart rates.

Recent findings suggest that overall, heart rate monitoring is an excellent training tool—but there are a few downsides. For one, it’s a little fickle. Your BPM can drift up or down depending on how much coffee you’ve had (caffeine raises it); ambient temperature; your hydration status; your plasma volume; how rested you are; and where you are in your menstrual cycle. It can also drift up within the same ride, especially when it’s hot.

In a recent development, pairing HR and RPE tracking gives you a more complete picture of your effort. If you’re performing tempo intervals at a target heart rate of 150 BPM and your RPE is around 5, you’re on the money. If you’re performing those same intervals but working at an RPE of 8 to hit that same heart rate, that’s a sign that you’re not recovered and should do an easier workout. There’s also some lag time between the moment you increase intensity and the moment your heart rate reflects it, so it’s not the best tool for high-intensity efforts.

You can monitor your heart rate with a chest strap or wrist-based heart rate monitor via your sports watch. Wrist-based sensors on smartwatches and fitness trackers can be less accurate for cyclists, according to some research. That may be due to the optical sensors having less consistent contact with our wrists as we bend it to grasp our bars.

Great for: The most accurate measure of your effort.

Equipment needed: A power meter and a compatible bike computer.

Sources indicate that power equals work over time. In cycling, your work rate is described as watts of energy produced: Being able to produce a lot of power for your size makes you faster on the bike. Monitoring your watts with a power meter gives you instant feedback about how hard you’re working.

Power training generally revolves around your functional threshold power, or the wattage you can produce for a one-hour time trial, which is a fundamental benchmark for fitness. A common protocol for determining your FTP is performing a 20-minute time trial and multiplying that average wattage by 0.95, since your hour-long wattage would be about 5 percent lower, according to Allen.

The beauty of power is that it is absolute: You are either producing 350 watts on those hill repeats, or you’re not. If you’re not hitting your intended watts for a given workout, it’s time to rest.

Though power is more precise than heart rate, it’s worthwhile to combine the two, as heart rate represents your body’s response to the work you’re doing. Your heart rate should rise and fall in line with your power output. When your power is low and your heart rate is high, it’s recovery time. If you’re serious about training to the point that you’ve hired a coach, a power meter is a good investment.

Great for: Understanding when you need more recovery time.

Equipment needed: An Oura ring, Whoop strap, or specific HRV tracking device.

HRV is a relatively fresh player in the performance tracking sphere. Unlike heart rate, which you watch in real time, HRV is one that you track once a day, preferably first thing in the morning (or if you wear an Oura ring or Whoop strap, you’ll see your average overnight score).

HRV is a good indicator of your recovery and/or readiness. It may seem counterintuitive, but a fit, rested, healthy heart should not beat consistently like a metronome. Instead, it should nimbly respond to input from your sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) nervous system.

High variability (reflected in a higher HRV score) indicates that you’re ready to go and capable of adapting to your environment and respond to exercise demands to perform well. Low variability between beats can be a sign of stress, fatigue, and inflammation—all things that can follow training too hard with too little recovery.

In a recent development, HRV is specific to each person and naturally declines with age. Though high numbers are considered “better,” high is relative to your own baseline. One person’s high HRV might be 125 while another’s high might be 55.

Recent findings suggest that referenced regularly, HRV scores will help you track fitness gains. For example, you’ll typically see HRV measurements decrease (become more negative) during long, heavy training blocks. Then you should see a rebound, where your HRV is significantly higher, after a recovery period. An upward trend over time means you’re getting fitter. A downward trend means you’re training too hard and or under too much stress without proper rest and recovery. When using HRV, it’s crucial not to put too much weight on a single day’s reading, but rather to look at trends and averages over a few days.

In a recent development, you can buy individual HRV monitors like straps and finger clip sensors, but if you’re going to track HRV, you should also track resting heart rate, sleep, and training load and/or activity levels, so you can put it into context. So, a device like a Whoop strap or Oura ring are the way to go, because they automatically put HRV into context of the whole picture. (If you work with a coach, they can as well).

Industry observers note that do you need to track HRV to become a better rider? Of course not. You can generally tell when you need a rest day by feel. But if you routinely train hard and like to dial in your training and lifestyle habits for optimum recovery and training readiness, this is a useful metric to use. It can be especially helpful if you’re trying to establish healthy habits like cutting back on alcohol and getting more sleep, because those types of lifestyle factors show up swiftly in HRV scores.

According to recent reports, all this measuring and monitoring doesn’t do much good unless you apply it to specific training purposes—that is, training at different effort levels to build specific types of fitness. That’s where training zones come in. Different coaches break down training zones differently, but in general you’ll see effort levels spread out over five to seven zones that range from recovery to max effort. For example, here are five classic training zones:.

Sources indicate that you need to ride easy so your body can heal, adapt, and get stronger and fitter. Zone 1 rides should feel ridiculously easy. Your only goal is to boost your circulation and promote repair and recovery. These rides hover at one or two on the RPE scale.

According to recent reports, zone 2 is all about aerobic effort. Endurance rides require enough energy to feel like exercise, but still let you carry a conversation, cruise for hours, and enjoy the ride. These efforts stimulate mitochondrial growth and build capillaries and fat-burning capacity. Zone 2 rides are done at an RPE of three to four.

According to recent reports, efforts in Zone 3 are just above your comfort level, so you’re breathing faster and working harder than you would on a typical aerobic, endurance ride. You’re not working so hard, however, that you can’t sustain your effort for a long period of time. Steady Zone 3 tempo efforts improve your body’s ability to clear and use lactic acid, so they also help raise your lactate threshold. They’re done at an RPE of five to six.

Sources indicate that if VO2 max is your roof, lactate threshold—the point at which you start working anaerobically—is your drop ceiling. Training in Zone 4, which is right at that point, helps you hit higher intensities before you bump into that overhang. These efforts are done at an RPE of seven to eight.

To raise your VO2max, the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use, you need to push yourself as far into the red as you can go. Zone 5 efforts are done full throttle—a nine to 10 on the RPE scale. Because they’re so hard, they’re also very short, generally lasting three to five minutes.

According to recent reports, here is a sample of basic training zones that incorporate the metrics above. Some coaches will break these down and expand them further or use other metrics such as percent of lactate threshold heart rate as a guide.

Zone 4Training Type: Lactate Threshold.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.
  • This pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Side stitch, stomach cramp, side ache — whatever you wanna call it, that mid-run pain in your tum can seriously *cramp* your runner’s high.

This pesky prob that plagues runners and athletes all over has a scientific name: Exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP). Though experts don’t know exactly what causes it, they have some ideas and tips about how to stop it.

Before you double-over during your next marathon, here’s what to know.

That fateful stab in your side is most likely to happen during exercise where your upper bod indicates tight and upright for an extended period, such as when you run, jog, bike, hike, play soccer, etc.

According to recent reports, this common prob has been around for ages — the first historical mention is from ancient Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder. Yet, scientists still haven’t reached a consensus on its exact cause. We know that it affects up to 70% of runners each year.

It’s also more likely to occur on the right side.

A stiff spine or poor posture (according to older research from 2010) could contribute to side stitches – but TBH, the pros don’t know for sure.

According to a 2022 review, researchers also think a side stitch might be caused by your right foot hitting the ground while you breathe out, irritating a phrenic nerve. Researchers think this, in turn, may bother the lining of your abdomen (particularly on the lower right side). Since most people are right-foot dominant, this is one possible explanation.

Experts also theorize that it could be triggered by the boost of blood flow around the diaphragm when running.

Furthermore, fueling up before a substantial race is excellent — but eating or drinking large quantities right before running may boost your risk of getting a side stitch, anecdotal reports suggest.

When a side stitch strikes, don’t stress – there are steps you can take, including:.

To stop a side stitch before it begins, here are some ideas FTW:.

Side stitches are usually harmless. But it’s always a good idea to visit a pro if you experience any of the following probs:.

In a recent development, side stitches are a common issue and not typically the reason for concern. Though pros don’t know what causes them, they think challenges with breathing, posture, or nerves may play a role.

In a recent development, consider working on your running form or breathing to reduce the risk of experiencing a side stitch. Staying hydrated and avoiding huge meals pre-run may also help. Consider working with a physical therapist or personal trainer if your complications persist.

If you experience pain under your breastbone when running, visit a doctor asap.

#9756. Don’t Let a Flat Tire End Your Ride. Here’s What I Carry in My Ride-Rescue Kit

📅 28 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1444 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Don’t Let a Flat Tire End Your Ride. Here’s What I Carry in My Ride-Rescue Kit

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that there are so many options out there when setting up a flat tire kit.
  • Building the right kit can make the difference between fixing the bike mid-ride and needing an unexpected pickup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that there are so many options out there when setting up a flat tire kit. During my time in bike shops I sold every flat kit you could imagine—from the basic prepackaged flat repair kits to repair kits that could fix almost anything on the bike. When you have the right pieces of gear, it can make the difference between an easy roadside fix and finding a proposal B to get home.

Building the right kit can make the difference between fixing the bike mid-ride and needing an unexpected pickup. One key is bringing the things you need and not what you don’t—then knowing how to use the tools in your kit.

Industry observers note that even on bikes you’ve had for a while it can be worth revisiting what’s sitting in your flat pack. Below I’ll walk you through what’s in my basic flat kit, why I pick those pieces, and why you should intermittently check out your flat pack to prevent any roadside surprises.

In a recent development, the tire levers are the foundation of any good flat repair kit—after all, you won’t be able to fix a flat very well if you can’t get the tire off and back on. I’ve gone through many different lever options over the years in my own flat kits, as well as from my time running a bike shop. The tire levers I swear by are the Pedro’s yellow tire levers. They are burly enough to be reliable and durable—I’m rarely worried about snapping a Pedro’s lever even on a tight tire.

The one thing many people don’t think about with levers is that sometimes you drop them or put them down when you’re trying to manage the roadside repair. The Pedro’s levers are easy to find thanks to their bright yellow color.

One runner-up is the tire lever from Muc-Off. They are similar in size, durability, and come in bright and easy to find colors. Personally I have not had the same amount of time using Muc-Off levers compared to the Pedro’s levers. One final tip: don’t use metal levers. Yes, they are burly, but they can easily damage rims when trying to get a tire off—especially carbon.

According to recent reports, the traditional tube you may have gotten the last time you stopped in your local shop while picking up a tube to fix a flat at home is a great option to put in your flat pack, but there are other options. TPU and latex tubes are popular because of their light weight and small packed size.

According to recent reports, I typically go with a standard tube on most of my flat kits. This is because I typically ride all year round and some of those lighter and more packable materials for tubes are more sensitive to temperature. If you’re a fair-weather rider, however, it can be worth considering a TPU or latex tube. Just remember to double-check that both the tube and valve size are correct for the wheels you are using.

Recent findings suggest that one note on checking out your tubes: check to make sure the tube is in good condition every few months. I was on a ride recently where someone got a flat and his multitool was against the tube in his saddle bag. The multitool rubbed a hole into the side of the tube making it useless. He mentioned he had not inspected that tube in at least a year. Luckily we had an extra tube for him and could keep rolling, but a quick check could have prevented him pulling a tube from someone else’s flat kit.

According to recent reports, similar to tire levers, I’ve used many different inflators over the years. My favorites to use are either the PDW CO2 inflator or the Muc-Off Inflator. These two options are durable and are easy to use with gloves on—which is especially helpful as we get into some cooler temperatures.

I carry two cans of CO2 because I’ve run into several experiences before where one ends up not being enough. It could be because I used one to try to add a burst of air in the hopes my tubeless system would fill the hole with sealant and I could go on my way. I’ve also had user error experiences where I simply didn’t get the canister on correctly and most or all of the air rushed out of the canister. In any case, they don’t take up much space, but having a backup is a key piece of the flat kit.

In a recent development, there are other inflation options you can go with too. Electronic pumps have been growing in popularity over the last few years, with test editor Dan Chabanov recently calling out the Cycplus AS2 Ultra Electric Inflator as his inflator of choice. I typically add a frame-mounted pump on longer rides, because these can’t run out of battery and as long as you can still pump you won’t run out of available air.

You’d be surprised what you can fix with a few zip ties. I’ve used these packable and inexpensive additions to fix issues like broken bottle cage bolts and broken cable and housing guides. I’ve had friends who have reattached things like derailleurs and saddle bags with a few strategically placed zip ties.

When I ride I typically carry a $10 bill and a single dollar bill. I know $11 seems like a random amount of money to carry on the bike. But the single and the ten serve two different purposes. A single dollar bill works as a great tire boot if you have a large gash in your tire. Simply put the dollar bill inside the tire against the gash before putting the tube in. If you run tubeless you can apply a little sealant from inside the tire to the dollar bill to help it stick better against the tire. Then when you inflate your tube, the pressure of the tube inside the tire will keep the dollar bill in place. The dollar bill will protect the tube from the elements and the road surface outside the tire.

The ten-dollar bill is your backup plan. I’ve been on rides before where I underestimated the amount of hydration and nutrition I needed to get through an effort. Having a few dollars for a gas station or convenience store refuel stop has dragged me out of the hole more than once. Most places these days take digital forms of payment like Apple Pay, but if you’re riding in more remote areas cash can be king.

A multitool that has the basic Allen keys and screwdriver that you’ll need is essential. If it has sizes 4, 5, and 6 you’ll be able to take care of most roadside fixes or adjustments you might ride into.

I personally like to bring a multitool with a chain breaker because I’ve had to fix a chain more than once on a ride. If fixing a chain is something you want to be prepared for on your ride, consider bringing a quick link that is compatible with your chain. They are another small and relatively inexpensive addition to your flat kit that can save plenty of headaches. A broken chain doesn’t have to be the end of your ride if you have the tools and the knowledge to piece it back together.

Different bikes have different ways to carry all this stuff. Some bikes have internal frame storage, some saddles have integrated mounts for certain bags, and some bikes have dropper posts that are only compatible with select saddle bags. On really short road rides I’ve even just thrown the basics of my flat kit in a jersey pocket. Personally, I typically put my flat repair kit into a frame bag, saddle bag, or utilize the internal frame storage so I can keep the extra weight and bulk off my body. If you have any essentials in your flat kit that I don’t include in mine let me know in the comments below.

Sources indicate that jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
